chunks: "I2C is defined relative to the supply rather than at fixed voltages.
A device sees a low below 30% of its V DD and a high above 70% of its V DD , and an I2C output pulls low to at most 0. 4 volts when sinking 3 milliamps.
The high level isn't driven at all: it's whatever rail the pull-up resistor goes to, so it equals the bus supply. The common bus voltages are 3. 3 volts, 1.
8 volts and 5 volts, with some 2. 5 volts and 1. 2 volts. At 3. 3 volts that means a low is anything under about 1 volts and a high is anything over about 2.
3 volts, which leaves roughly 0. 6 volts of noise margin on the low side and 1 volts on the high side. At 5 volts the thresholds are 1. 5 volts and 3. 5 volts.
The gotcha is mixing voltages. A 5 volts device needs 3. 5 volts to see a high, so if you put it on a 3. 3 volts bus it may never see a valid high. And pulling a 3.
3 volts bus up into a 1. 8 volts part can exceed its maximum rating.
For anything with different supplies I'd either run everything at the same voltage or put a level translator in, with a pull-up on each side."
